_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Romania covering Dacian kingdom (Decebalus), Roman conquest (Trajan 106 CE, Dacia Traiana), Romance language survival, medieval principalities (Wallachia/Moldavia/Transylvania), Ottoman suzerainty, Russian influence, union 1859, Kingdom 1881, WWI (joined Entente 1916, gained Transylvania/Bessarabia), Greater Romania 1918-40, WWII (Antonescu allied with Axis, switched 1944), communist era (1945-89, Gheorghiu-Dej, Ceaușescu), Revolution 1989 (violent, Ceaușescus executed), EU/NATO 2004/2007.

religion.note: Romanian Orthodox Church (autocephalous, majority); church and national identity intertwined (vs Ottoman Islam, Catholic Hungary, atheist communism); post-communist religious revival; Maramureș wooden churches (UNESCO); Greek Catholic/Uniate (banned under communism 1948-89, returned property disputes); monastic traditions (Voroneț 'Sistine Chapel of the East'); low secularism compared to Western Europe

ethnic_groups.name: Romanian
ethnic_groups.notes: Romance language island in Slavic sea (descended from Roman Dacia); Romanianness (românitate/latinity) central to identity; Transylvania emotionally central (united 1918, lost 1940-45, regained); diaspora ~4M (Italy ~1.2M, Spain ~800k, Germany ~800k, UK ~400k, massive post-EU accession emigration)

ethnic_groups.name: Hungarian (Székely)
ethnic_groups.notes: ~1.2M; Transylvania (Hunedoara/Harghita/Covasna counties, majority in some); Székely identity (distinct Hungarian subgroup); autonomy demands (contentious); UDMR party; bilingual areas; Trianon legacy (Hungary lost Transylvania 1920)

ethnic_groups.name: Roma
ethnic_groups.notes: Official 3.4%, estimated 5-10% (many don't declare, ~1.8M+); most marginalised; slavery until 1856 (500 years); extreme poverty; inter-ethnic violence; gold/music traditions; Ceaușescu forced assimilation; discrimination pervasive

ethnic_groups.name: German
ethnic_groups.notes: Transylvanian Saxons (7th largest city Sibiu/Hermannstadt); most emigrated to Germany post-1989 (Ceaușescu sold ethnic Germans for hard currency, ~200k); Banat Swabians; Klaus Iohannis (ethnic German president)

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Turkish/Tatar (Dobrogea), Serbs, Lipovans (Russian Old Believers, Danube Delta), Greeks, Jews (pre-WWII ~750k, Holocaust ~380k murdered, Iron Guard/Antonescu, emigration to Israel post-1947, now ~3k); Bulgarians

independence.from: Ottoman Empire (declared; recognised at Congress of Berlin 1878); modern state: Principalities united 1859

country_profile.notes_unique: 1989 Revolution (only violent Eastern European communist overthrow, December 16-25, Timișoara sparked, Bucharest battles, ~1,100 dead, Securitate snipers, Ceaușescus fled, captured, kangaroo trial, executed by firing squad Christmas Day); Nicolae Ceaușescu (dictator 1965-89, Stalinist personality cult, 'Conducător', systematization destroyed villages, demolished Bucharest for Palace of Parliament/world's 2nd largest building, debt repayment impoverished nation, abortion ban pronatalism, orphanages catastrophe); Vlad Țepeș/Vlad the Impaler (Dracula inspiration, Wallachian prince, impaled Ottoman invaders, Romanian hero); Transylvania (Hungarian for 400+ years, awarded to Romania 1920 Trianon, emotional/symbolic core of Greater Romania); Palace of Parliament (2nd largest building in world, 1,100 rooms, Ceaușescu's megalomania, 700 architects, 40k demolished homes); Danube Delta (UNESCO, 2nd largest in Europe, biodiversity); corruption (most corrupt EU state, CVM Cooperation and Verification Mechanism since 2007, Schengen blocked, progress slow); orphanage scandal (AIDS epidemic among abandoned babies, international adoptions, Ceaușescu's pronatalism legacy); brain drain (doctors/IT workers emigrate en masse post-EU)

current_leader.name: Marcel Ciolacu
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: PSD (Social Democrats); coalition with PNL (grand coalition); centrist technocratic governance; December 2024 election chaos (first round canceled by Constitutional Court amid Russian interference allegations)

head_of_state.name: Klaus Iohannis
head_of_state.title: President
head_of_state.notes: PNL; ethnic German (Transylvanian Saxon); former Sibiu mayor; two terms; anti-corruption advocate; EU/NATO integration; tense cohabitation with PSD governments; extended his term beyond December 2024 due to election cancellation crisis; unpopular at end of term (foreign trips, inaction)

former_leaders.name: Ion Iliescu
former_leaders.notes: FSN/PDSR; Ceaușescu Communist Party official who broke with regime; took power after 1989 (National Salvation Front); Jiu Valley miners violence 1990-91; slow reforms; convicted 2019 for crimes against humanity (1989 post-revolution violence, 862 dead); controversial founding father

former_leaders.name: Traian Băsescu
former_leaders.notes: PD-L; ship captain background; populist; anti-corruption rhetoric; impeachment attempts (2007, 2012, survived); suspended twice; confrontational; EU accession 2007; polarizing

former_leaders.name: Adrian Năstase
former_leaders.notes: PSD; moderniser; EU integration progress; corruption charges post-premiership (convicted 2012, imprisoned, first ex-PM jailed); suicide attempt 2012

former_leaders.name: Nicolae Ceaușescu
former_leaders.notes: Communist dictator; personality cult ('Conducător', Genius of the Carpathians); independence from Moscow (condemned 1968 Czechoslovakia invasion, gained Western approval); 1980s austerity (repaid foreign debt, impoverished citizens, food/heat rationing); systematization (demolished 8,000 villages); abortion ban (pronatalism, orphanages); Securitate terror; executed Christmas 1989; hated tyrant

former_leaders.name: Carol II
former_leaders.notes: Scandalous personal life (mistress Magda Lupescu); royal dictatorship 1938; abdicated 1940 (pressure from Iron Guard/Antonescu); Greater Romania era; flawed democracy interwar period

910.name: Dacians & Roman Dacia
910.description: The Dacian civilisation, centred in the Carpathian Mountains, rivalled Rome under King Decebalus. Trajan's conquest (101–106 CE) created the province of Dacia, whose romanisation became the foundation of Romanian identity and the Latin-derived Romanian language.

sub_clusters.name: Dacian Kingdoms
sub_clusters.description: The Getae-Dacian civilisation, King Burebista's unification of Dacian tribes (82–44 BCE), the mountain fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains (UNESCO), and King Decebalus's resistance to Roman expansion culminating in the Dacian Wars (101–106 CE).

920.name: Migration Period & Vlach Emergence
920.description: After the Roman withdrawal, successive migratory waves (Goths, Huns, Slavs, Avars, Bulgars, Magyars, Cumans) crossed the territory. The Romanised population (Vlachs) survived in mountain regions, gradually emerging as a distinct ethnic group.

sub_clusters.name: Barbarian Migrations & Slavic Influence
sub_clusters.description: Gothic, Hunnic, Avar, and Slavic migrations through the Carpathian-Danubian region. Slavic settlement influenced the Romanian language (40% of vocabulary) and Orthodox Christianity. The First and Second Bulgarian Empires extended influence over parts of the territory.

920.name: Principalities of Wallachia & Moldavia
920.description: The founding of the principalities of Wallachia (c. 1290, Basarab I) and Moldavia (1359, Bogdan I) created the two pillars of Romanian statehood. Mircea the Elder and Stephen the Great defended their lands against Ottoman expansion.

sub_clusters.name: Founding of Wallachia & Mircea the Elder
sub_clusters.description: Basarab I's defeat of the Hungarian king at Posada (1330) secured Wallachian independence. Mircea the Elder (r. 1386–1418) expanded the principality and fought the Ottomans at Rovine (1395) and Nicopolis (1396).

930.name: Ottoman Suzerainty & Phanariot Era
930.description: Wallachia and Moldavia became Ottoman vassal states, retaining internal autonomy but paying heavy tribute. Michael the Brave briefly united all three Romanian lands (1600). The Phanariot era (1711–1821) saw Greek-origin princes governing under Ottoman direction.

sub_clusters.name: Michael the Brave & First Romanian Union
sub_clusters.description: Michael the Brave (Mihai Viteazul) briefly united Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania (1600) — a foundational moment in Romanian national mythology. His assassination (1601) ended the union, but it inspired later unification movements.

sub_clusters.description: Ottoman control tightened through appointed Phanariot Greek princes (1711 in Moldavia, 1716 in Wallachia). Fiscal exploitation, boyar resistance, and the Phanariots' paradoxical role in transmitting Enlightenment ideas. Tudor Vladimirescu's 1821 uprising ended Phanariot rule.

940.name: National Awakening & Unification
940.description: The Transylvanian School's assertion of Roman Dacian continuity, the 1848 Wallachian revolution, the union of Wallachia and Moldavia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza (1859), and Romanian independence won in the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78).

940.name: Kingdom of Romania & Belle Époque
940.description: King Carol I proclaimed the Kingdom of Romania (1881). Rapid modernisation, the Bucharest Belle Époque, the peasant revolt of 1907, Romania's entry into WWI (1916), and the creation of Greater Romania (1918) uniting Transylvania, Bukovina, and Bessarabia.

950.name: Interwar Romania & WWII
950.description: Greater Romania faced the rise of the fascist Iron Guard, King Carol II's royal dictatorship, territorial losses (1940), alliance with Nazi Germany, the switch of sides (August 1944), and participation in the liberation of Transylvania.

960.name: 1989 Revolution & Democratic Romania
960.description: The Romanian Revolution of December 1989 — the only violent overthrow of a communist regime in Eastern Europe — executed Ceaușescu. Post-revolutionary Romania underwent a painful transition to democracy and market economy, culminating in EU accession (2007).

Ion Iliescu's controversial presidency, the Mineriad violence, and the slow democratic and economic transition.
